answers.answer: Embedded means the engine executes inside the application process: code calls SQLite directly for SQL rather than sending queries across a process/network boundary to a separate database server. Persistent data lives in a local file; in-memory databases are also supported. It still offers relational tables, joins, indexes and transactions. Application-local data benefits from direct local access and fewer services, including offline use. Many application servers updating shared data across a network make locality, shared access and competing writes harder; a client/server database is often a better fit. SQLite may serve many users through an application server accessing its local database. User count or size alone does not specify where access happens or how much work competes to write; measure write contention, transaction duration and representative queries, and check capacity. Independent device copies do not synchronize automatically: additional software and conflict handling are needed.

evidence.quote: The engine runs inside your application's process. Your code calls SQLite directly, rather than sending queries to a separate database server.
A persistent database lives in a local file. SQLite also supports in-memory databases.
SQLite stores data in tables and supports SQL queries, joins, indexes, and transactions.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
Sharing changes between independent device or server copies requires additional software. Local transactions do not resolve conflicting edits elsewhere.

answers.answer: Type affinity guides conversions in ordinary tables; individual values have storage classes, and an integer declaration can retain text that cannot convert. STRICT tables require values to fit their declared types after permitted conversions, except ANY columns. Primary keys identify rows; UNIQUE restricts duplicates; NOT NULL rejects missing values; CHECK rejects false conditions. Required values need explicit NOT NULL because CHECK alone does not establish that missing values are invalid, and foreign-key references can be null unless forbidden. Foreign keys constrain references to existing rows. Before a transaction, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection, query PRAGMA foreign_keys and verify 1. Atomicity makes the grouped database changes all-or-none; consistency preserves defined rules; isolation controls concurrent visibility and write coordination, normally hiding incomplete changes; durability preserves committed work according to configured guarantees. Commit accepts grouped work; rollback cancels it, avoiding partial transaction effects. Constraints define the rules consistency must preserve, and correct transaction logic remains necessary because isolation does not eliminate races or lock waits. Rollback journaling records original data for undo; WAL records changes in a separate log. Durability settings that defer persistent flushing may lose recent commits after power failure, and guarantees also depend on reliable filesystem locking and storage honoring flushes. An external network action is outside the database transaction, so rollback cannot undo it.

evidence.quote: Ordinary tables use affinity to guide conversions; each value has a storage class, such as integer, text or null. A declared integer column can retain text that cannot be converted.
These enforce stronger type checks. Values must fit the declared type after permitted conversions, except columns explicitly declared ANY.
Primary keys identify rows; UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values and CHECK rejects false conditions. Combine CHECK with NOT NULL when a missing value must also be invalid.

Constrain references to existing rows; null references are allowed unless separately forbidden. Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
All changes succeed together, or none take effect.
Changes preserve the rules you defined.
Groups database changes. Commit accepts them; rollback cancels them.
Controls concurrent visibility and write coordination. Normal settings hide incomplete changes, but do not remove application races, lock waits or the need for correct transaction logic.
Committed changes survive failures according to the configured guarantees. This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.
Settings that delay flushing committed changes to persistent storage can lose recent transactions after a power failure.
Only database work inside the transaction is covered. Rollback does not reverse an external network side effect.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change.
Records changes in a separate log.

answers.answer: Several connections, even from different processes on the same machine, can exist, but each database permits only one active writer. Write contention means competing work needs writing access that cannot be held simultaneously. SQLITE_BUSY means a connection could not obtain required access. Short write transactions reduce how long unrelated writes are held up; avoid waiting for a network request while holding a write transaction. A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention, but handle failed attempts and retry the transaction where necessary. Waiting cannot create writer capacity or guarantee success. Rollback-journal mode saves original data for undoing an interrupted change, and readers and writers can block one another. WAL saves changes in a separate log so readers retain stable snapshots while a writer commits. A checkpoint transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long readers can delay that progress and grow the log. WAL still has one writer; its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine. Respect local-file access permissions and reliable filesystem locking, and do not treat WAL as a shared database mechanism for remote application servers. The lesson does not specify detailed shared-file configuration or which busy failures require whole-transaction retries.

evidence.quote: SQLite supports multiple connections, including connections from different processes on the same machine. But each database allows only one active writer at a time.

A connection can receive this result when it cannot obtain required access. A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention; some failures require retrying the transaction. Waiting does not create another writer or guarantee success.
Keep write transactions short. A transaction that waits on a network request can hold up unrelated writes.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change. In this mode, readers and writers can block each other.
Records changes in a separate log. Readers can continue using a stable snapshot while a writer commits changes.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.
This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.

answers.answer: An index is an additional structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows. A query plan is the chosen sequence of access and processing steps for filtering, joins, sorting and aggregation. For owner filtering with time ordering, a candidate is a composite index ordered by owner then time, inferred from the instruction to match index columns and their order to filters and requested ordering. Inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see the selected access/processing steps, and measure representative queries instead of assuming that candidate must be used. Small tables or broad queries may reasonably use a scan. Indexes consume space and add write maintenance; local queries still cost CPU, storage I/O and memory. Without a separate service, the application and host must manage filesystem permissions, free space and recovery. Coordinate schema migrations with application versions and active access; some require table rebuilding and copying data. Use a supported consistent backup for an active database, retain backups according to recovery needs, and test restoration and application usability. During WAL use, committed state may remain in the log, so copying only the main database can omit required data. The supported consistent backup addresses that requirement; merely possessing a file does not prove consistency or recovery time. Gap: the lesson gives no procedure or sufficient criteria for a verified quiescent-state copy, so I cannot establish from it when such a copy is safe; lack of current writes alone does not establish that all committed WAL state is in the main file.

evidence.quote: Chooses access and processing steps for joins, filtering, sorting and aggregation. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows those steps.
An additional structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows. Match columns and their order to actual filters and requested ordering; a composite index contains multiple columns.
A scan can be preferable for small tables or broad queries. The planner need not use an index merely because it exists. Measure representative queries.
Local execution still uses CPU, storage I/O and memory. Indexes take space and add write maintenance; avoiding a network call does not make expensive work free.
A migration changes stored structure. Coordinate it with application versions and active access; some changes require rebuilding a table and copying data.
Use a supported consistent backup method for an active database. Committed data may still be in the WAL, so copying only the main file can omit required state.
Manage access permissions and free space. Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability. A backup file alone does not prove consistency or recovery time.

answers.answer: SQLite is a plausible choice for one host with short occasional writes: data stays close to code, fewer services need operation, and writers can plausibly take turns. WAL can overlap readers with a writer, but cannot add simultaneous writers. Several application servers sustaining concurrent writes to shared data are a poorer fit: many machines need shared access and competing writes may not take turns acceptably, while WAL requires same-machine processes. I would favor evaluating a client/server database for that case, rather than assuming a network-shared SQLite file fixes it. In either case, define required types and constraints, verify foreign-key enforcement per connection, use correct transactions, inspect query plans and index costs, and provide consistent backups with restore testing. Before deciding, verify data locality and access paths, write contention and transaction duration, whether writes can take turns, representative query behavior, long-read/checkpoint behavior, storage capacity and reliable locking/flush behavior. Clarify required durability, recovery needs/time, permissions, migration coordination and whether independent copies need synchronization/conflict handling. User count or size alone is insufficient. Gap: the lesson supplies no numeric thresholds, workload measurements, retry policy or complete backup procedure, so these choices remain conditional on verified requirements and measurements.

evidence.quote: Direct local access, fewer services to run, and a database that can travel with the application.
One writer per database, responsibility for local files, and additional work if data must synchronize across machines.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns. SQLite can still be suitable behind an application server with local storage.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
The planner need not use an index merely because it exists. Measure representative queries.
Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability.
Explain where the data lives, who writes it, and how failures are handled. Those requirements make the choice defensible.
